She's saying it looks like companies charge more just because the product is for women, that the gender itself is the reason for the price. That's the claim I want to test. And it doesn't hold up. Here's the strongest evidence. Economists at Chicago Booth and Northwestern, Sara Moshari, Anna Tuchman, and Natasha Vashravelu, studied exactly this. At Pinktax, they pulled scanner data from nearly 40,000 US stores for personal care products. Soap, shampoo, deodorant, razors, shaving cream, you name it. Now with the research part out of the way, play devil's advocate with me. Say you did find two products that were genuinely identical. Same manufacturer, same ingredients. Even then, the price isn't just the cost of what's inside. Price is also marketing. Price is also competition. And above all, price is supply and demand. If demand's higher for the women's version, given the supply is the same, it drives the price up. That's not sexism. That's economics. And if you really think pricing is just pick a gender, charge them more, look at where men pay more. Life insurance. Men pay more. Openly. Because we die younger, so we are a bigger risk to insure.
